title: Demonstrate basic knowledge of welfare issues relating to wildlife

lessons.title: Wildlife classifications, legislation and facilities
lessons.html:
Classifying wildlife

Animal welfare workers increasingly deal with wild animals: injured animals brought to rehabilitation centres, animals in zoos, sanctuaries and breeding facilities, and wildlife kept illegally as pets. Wildlife can be classified in several ways:

  • By origin: indigenous (native to South Africa) or alien (introduced from elsewhere).
  • By conservation status: from least concern to endangered and critically endangered, as listed nationally and by the IUCN Red List.
  • By legal protection: listed species under the Threatened or Protected Species (TOPS) regulations of the National Environmental Management: Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004, and categories under provincial conservation laws.
  • By management setting: free-ranging, managed on game farms, or held in captivity.

Relevant legislation

  • Biodiversity Act 10 of 2004 and TOPS: permits for keeping, breeding, moving and selling listed species.
  • Provincial conservation laws: permits to keep, transport or rehabilitate wild animals.
  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962: applies to wild animals in captivity or under human control.
  • Performing Animals Protection Act 24 of 1935: for wild animals used in performances or films.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984: for diseases such as rabies and foot-and-mouth disease.

General requirements in different facilities

FacilityMain welfare requirements
Zoos and aquariaEnclosures meeting species needs, enrichment, vet care, education role
Rehabilitation centresMinimal human contact, preparation for release, permits
SanctuariesLifelong care for non-releasable animals, no breeding or trade
Breeding facilities and game farmsSpace, natural diet, social groups, safe handling
Transport and holdingCrates, bomas, quiet, shade, water

lessons.title: Welfare requirements and alien animals
lessons.html:
Welfare requirements for wildlife

Wild animals are not domesticated; they do not get used to people in the way a dog or cow does. Stress is a major welfare problem and can kill.

  • Space and shelter: enough room to move, hide and escape the sight of people and other species.
  • Diet: species-appropriate food; a browser needs browse, not only lucerne. Poor diet in captive animals leads to bone and dental disease.
  • Water: clean and always available.
  • Social needs: herd animals such as antelope need companions; solitary species such as leopards need to be housed alone.
  • Behavioural needs: foraging, climbing, digging, swimming and enrichment to prevent pacing and other abnormal behaviour.
  • Health care: a wildlife vet, parasite control, safe immobilisation and quarantine.
  • Handling: minimal, planned and quiet. Risks include capture myopathy and overheating.

Public interaction concerns

Cub petting, walking with predators and selfies with wild animals are controversial. Young animals may be removed from their mothers early, and adult animals may later be sold or used in breeding. Welfare workers should understand the concerns and advise the public on responsible tourism.

Alien animals in the wildlife industry

Alien species are used in the industry for hunting, venison and the pet trade. Examples include fallow deer, Himalayan tahr, and exotic birds and reptiles kept as pets. Concerns include:

  • Escape and establishment in the wild, competing with or hybridising with indigenous species.
  • Introduction of diseases and parasites.
  • Welfare of exotic pets kept without proper knowledge or conditions.

The alien and invasive species regulations under the Biodiversity Act control which alien species may be kept, and some require permits. Releasing an alien animal into the wild is not acceptable.

Key points

  • Wildlife is classified by origin, conservation status, legal protection and setting.
  • The Biodiversity Act (TOPS) and provincial laws govern keeping and moving wildlife.
  • Welfare needs include space, correct diet, social grouping, enrichment and minimal handling.
  • Public interaction with wild animals raises welfare concerns.
  • Alien animals can escape, spread disease and harm indigenous species; permits apply.
